analysis.one_liner: Requires a federal license to own a handgun or certain semiautomatic rifle and routes every sale through a licensed dealer with background checks and a record of sale.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Judiciary Committee without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required anyone who owns a handgun or a semiautomatic rifle that accepts a detachable magazine to get a federal firearm owner license — with a photo, fingerprints, a background check, and a fee of up to $10, renewable every five years. It would also require every sale or transfer of those guns to go through a licensed dealer, extend background checks to private sales, create a federal record of sale system, require owners to report lost or stolen guns, and penalize leaving a loaded gun where a child can reach it. Violations could carry up to 10 years in prison.
analysis.who_benefits: The general public, especially people exposed to gun violence, and law enforcement agencies, which would gain a license system and a federal record of sale to trace guns used in crime.

how_it_helps.text: Requires every owner of a handgun or semiautomatic rifle with a detachable magazine over 10 rounds to hold a license, with a fingerprint-based background check and safety criteria such as age 21 (with parental consent exceptions) and no recent violent offenses or involuntary commitment [S3].

Closes the private-sale loophole by requiring transfers between unlicensed people to be processed through a licensed dealer, with narrow exceptions for gifts within a family and short-term loans [S3].
Requires dealers to report each covered sale to a federal record of sale system and requires owners to report a lost or stolen gun within 72 hours, which helps police trace crime guns [S3].
Creates a firearm injury clearinghouse and requires federal studies of gun deaths and of 'smart gun' technology [S3].

Makes it a crime, punishable by up to 5 years, to keep a loaded firearm accessible to a child if the child uses it to kill or seriously injure someone, with exceptions for secured storage and lawful self-defense [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Gun owners, who would pay licensing fees, submit fingerprints and mental-health certifications, and face criminal penalties of up to 10 years for possessing a covered gun without a license; dealers, who must process private transfers; and taxpayers, who fund the federal licensing and record system.

drawbacks.text: The licensing scheme is broad: possessing a covered firearm without a license would be a crime punishable by up to 10 years, and even current owners would have had only two years to comply [S3].

Applicants must certify they were not patients in a mental health facility in the past five years and must authorize release of mental health records — requirements that objectors have argued could deter people from seeking mental health care and sweep in people who pose no danger [S3].

The bill repeals the existing federal prohibition on establishing a firearms registration system and creates a federal record of sale database, which gun owners and gun-rights groups have long opposed as a de facto registration of gun owners [S3].

The bill imposes paperwork and compliance costs on lawful owners and dealers, while its supporters offered no evidence in the bill itself that licensing would stop criminals who simply would not apply for a license [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would impose real burdens on millions of lawful gun owners — fees, fingerprints, mental-health disclosures, and prison exposure for noncompliance — in exchange for a licensing and tracing system aimed at keeping guns from prohibited people and helping police trace crime guns. The heaviest costs fall on owners of the roughly half of American guns covered by the definition; the public-safety payoff depends on how well the system is administered, and the bill's expansive mental-health provisions were its most questionable design choice.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never held a hearing or a vote, and it died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Senator Tammy Duckworth introduced the bill on July 25, 2019 [S1][S5].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S1][S5].
No other senator cosponsored the bill [S4].
The bill took no further legislative action for the rest of the Congress and never reached the Senate floor [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Gun owners and firearms dealers are better off, since no licensing, dealer-intermediary, or record-of-sale requirements were enacted; no new restrictions took effect for the public either.

for.name: Tammy Duckworth
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

against.name: Lindsey Graham
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee markup during the 116th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote and drew zero cosponsors from either party, so the record shows no roll-call or co-sponsorship pattern on which to judge a partisan split.

industries.note: Every sale or transfer of a covered firearm, including private sales, would have to be processed through a licensed dealer, who verifies the buyer's license and reports the sale — making dealers the mandatory channel for all covered gun transfers, presumably for a fee.

Manufacturers would face new reporting of production and sales figures to the Attorney General, and licensing requirements could dampen demand, but semiautomatic rifles and handguns remain fully legal to make and sell.
